t: Grand Slam Titles — Flattening Four Winner Columns Into One Count
o:
## Understanding the problem

Two tables: **Players**(player_id, player_name) and a wide **Championships**(year, Wimbledon, Fr_open, US_open, Au_open) holding one row per year where each tournament column stores the winning player_id. Every cell across the four tournament columns represents one title, so a player’s grand-slam total is simply the number of cells equal to their id. Players who appear in no cell must be excluded from the result.

**Example walkthrough:** player 1 (Nadal) owns Wimbledon 2018 and 2019, Fr_open 2018 through 2020, US_open 2018, Au_open 2018 — 7 titles. Player 2 (Federer) owns Wimbledon 2020, US_open 2019 and 2020, Au_open 2019 and 2020 — 5 titles. Player 3 (Novak) appears nowhere, so he is omitted. Expected columns: player_id, player_name, grand_slams_count.

The tables are tiny, so the challenge is semantic rather than performance: treat the four tournament columns symmetrically, count title cells rather than matched rows (one player can win several tournaments within the same year-row), and let inner-join semantics drop the zero-title players.
k: Each Championships row carries up to four titles — a player’s total equals the number of tournament cells holding their id, not the number of rows containing them.
Joining with player_id IN (Wimbledon, Fr_open, US_open, Au_open) fans a year-row out once per matching column, so COUNT(*) already counts titles.
An inner join (or an existence filter) removes zero-title players for free, and grouping by player_id alone is safe because player_name depends on the primary key.

a.i: Mirror the SQL shape SELECT p.player_name, COUNT(*) FROM Players p JOIN Championships c ON p.player_id IN (c.Wimbledon, c.Fr_open, c.US_open, c.Au_open) GROUP BY p.player_id. Drive the loop from the players: each player sweeps every championship row and all four tournament columns, incrementing a counter on matches, and survives only with a positive total. Allocation-light and very hard to get wrong.
s: For each player, iterate all Championships rows and each of the four tournament columns.
Increment the counter whenever a cell equals the player id.
Keep the (id, name, count) triple only if count > 0.
Return the collected triples in any order.
a.t: O(P · 4Y) — each of the P players is compared against every title cell across Y yearly rows

a.n: Approach 2: Unpivot into title records, aggregate, join back (title-first)
a.i: Mirror the UNION ALL unpivot: stack the four winner columns into one long list of title events, aggregate counts per winner (GROUP BY), then attach names by looking players up (JOIN). One pass over all 4Y cells builds the totals regardless of how many players exist, and the lookup pass filters zero-title players naturally through failed lookups. Flatten, aggregate, join — the shape interviewers want defended.
s: Flatten the four tournament columns of every row into a single stream of winner ids.
Aggregate counts per winner id in a hash map.
Iterate players, looking each id up in the map.
Emit (id, name, count) for hits; misses mean zero titles and are skipped.
Return the triples in any order.

c.python:
import pandas as pd

class Solution:
    def grand_slam_titles(self, players: pd.DataFrame, championships: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        cols = ['Wimbledon', 'Fr_open', 'US_open', 'Au_open']
        long_format = pd.concat([championships[c] for c in cols], ignore_index=True)
        counts = long_format.value_counts().reset_index()
        counts.columns = ['player_id', 'grand_slams_count']
        merged = counts.merge(players, on='player_id', how='inner')
        return merged[['player_id', 'player_name', 'grand_slams_count']]

a.t: O(4Y + P) expected — one hashed increment per title cell plus one lookup per player
a.sp: O(W) — one hash entry per distinct winner W

w:
## Wrap-up

Say the key sentence first: each of the four columns is a title, so we need a count of cells, not rows. Then offer both shapes — the compact IN-join and the UNION-ALL unpivot — and implement whichever reads better to you.

**Common pitfalls**

- Joining on year alone or aggregating the wide row directly: a player who wins three events in one year-row must contribute 3, so the join must fan out per matching column.
- LEFT JOIN from Players without a filter leaves zero-title players in the result; the problem forbids them, so use an inner join or an explicit existence check.
- Match the expected schema exactly: columns player_id, player_name, grand_slams_count, in that order.
- In procedural translations, remember the four columns are positional — iterate all four, not just one.

**Likely follow-ups:** rank winners by title count with deterministic tie-breaking, or produce per-tournament breakdowns.
